Foundations: know your true cost

Understand the difference between cost, price and profit, then calculate the true cost of one product or service, including your own time and overheads. You will also set up simple records and protect yourself from payment scams before you start changing prices.
Cost, price and profit: why so many sellers undercharge
Explain the difference between cost, price and profit in plain words
Identify the three common pricing mistakes small sellers make

Every sale has three numbers behind it. **Cost** is the money (and time) it takes you to make or buy the thing you sell. **Price** is what the customer pays you. **Profit** is what is left when you take cost away from price. If a pack of chin chin costs you ₦550 to make and you sell it for ₦800, your profit on that pack is ₦250. If you sell it for ₦500, you are not making a small profit: you are losing ₦50 on every pack, even if your purse feels full at the end of the day.

That last point surprises many people. Money coming in is called **revenue** or sales. Revenue is not profit. A woman can sell ₦40,000 of goods in a week and still be poorer than when she started, because the cost of those goods was higher than she realised. This course is about seeing your real numbers clearly, choosing a price on purpose, and then selling at that price with calm confidence.

Three mistakes that keep sellers poor

**Counting only materials.** Many sellers add up flour, sugar and oil, then stop. They forget packaging, transport to market, gas, phone data for WhatsApp orders, and most of all, their own hours of work.

**Copying the next seller's price.** The woman beside you may buy in bulk, use cheaper inputs, have no shop rent, or simply be losing money without knowing it. Her price tells you about the market, not about your cost.

**Never reviewing the price.** In Nigeria the cost of inputs such as flour, cooking gas and transport can change quickly. A price that gave a good profit six months ago can quietly turn into a loss if you never recalculate.

You will learn to fix each of these. Module 1 helps you find your true cost. Module 2 shows you how to turn that cost into a price using three methods: cost-plus, competitor-based and value-based pricing, and how discounts affect your profit. Module 3 is about the selling conversation, objections and daily records. Module 4 brings it together into a pricing sheet and a 90-day review plan.
The three prices every product has

It helps to picture three levels for any product or service. The first is your **price floor**: your true cost per item. Below this you lose money on every sale. The second is the **market range**: what similar products sell for around you, from the cheapest to the most expensive. The third is the **value ceiling**: the highest amount a customer would happily pay because of what your product does for them, such as saving time, looking good at an event, or tasting fresher than the rest.
Where a good price sits
Value ceiling: what buyers gladly pay
Market range: what others charge
Price floor: your true cost
A healthy price sits above your floor, inside or near the market range, and below what your best customers believe it is worth.

Your job is to choose a price that is **always above the floor**, makes sense against the market range, and moves closer to the value ceiling as your quality, reputation and service improve. A seller who only looks at the floor may price too low. A seller who only looks at competitors may price below her own cost. A seller who only dreams about value may price so high that no one buys. You need all three views.
Worked example: the busy seller who was losing money
For example, Ngozi sells small packs of chin chin to offices in Enugu. She charges ₦500 a pack because that is what another seller charges. All figures here are approximate and only for illustration.
She adds up one batch: ingredients and gas about ₦13,000, packaging about ₦2,000, transport and data about ₦2,000.
That is ₦17,000 for 40 packs, or ₦425 a pack. She thinks she makes ₦75 profit on each one.
Then she counts her time: about 5 hours of mixing, cutting, frying and packing. She values her time at about ₦1,000 an hour, so ₦5,000 per batch.
Her true cost is ₦22,000 for 40 packs, which is ₦550 a pack.
At ₦500 a pack she is giving away ₦50 of her labour on every sale. She is not running a business yet; she is subsidising her customers. Lesson 2 shows how to do this calculation step by step.
Why your time counts

If you do not pay yourself for your hours, the business looks profitable only because you are working for free. One day you may want to hire help, take a rest week or grow. If your price never included labour, you will not be able to afford any of these.
What a good price does for you
It covers every cost, including your time, so the business can keep going.
It leaves a profit you can save, reinvest in stock, or use to grow.
It gives you room to offer a planned discount without falling below cost.
It sends a message about quality: a price far below everyone else can make buyers suspicious.

Finding your true cost per item
Separate direct costs, labour and overhead
Set a fair hourly rate for your own labour

Your true cost is the total of everything it takes to produce one item or deliver one job. To find it, you sort your costs into three groups, add them for a whole batch (or a whole month), and then divide by the number of items you make. This lesson walks you through each group and two full examples, one for a product and one for a service.
Group 1: direct costs (materials and packaging)

**Direct costs** are things that go into, or onto, the product. If you make one more item, you use more of them. For food this is ingredients, cooking gas or charcoal, and packaging such as nylon, labels and containers. For a tailor it is thread, lining, zips, buttons and interfacing. For a reseller of shoes or bags it is the price you paid the wholesaler plus the cost of bringing the goods home.

Use what you actually paid, from your last receipts or market trip, not what you hope to pay. If you buy a 10 kg bag of flour and use 2 kg per batch, only count one fifth of the bag's price in each batch.
Group 2: your labour

**Labour** is the time you, and anyone who helps you, spend making and selling. Count shopping for inputs, preparing, producing, packing and delivering. To put a value on your hour, ask: what could I reasonably earn doing similar work for someone else? For example, if similar daily work in your area pays about ₦8,000 for an 8-hour day, your hour is worth about ₦1,000. If someone helps you and you pay them, their pay goes here too.
Labour is a cost, not your profit
Paying yourself for your hours is your wage. Profit is extra money the business earns on top of everyone's wages. Keeping the two separate tells you whether the business itself is healthy.
Group 3: overhead

**Overhead** is the cost of running the business that does not belong to one single item: stall or shop rent, market levy, electricity or generator fuel, phone data for WhatsApp orders, transport to market, POS charges and equipment wear. Add these up for a month, then share them across everything you make in that month. If your overhead is ₦20,000 a month and you make 400 packs, each pack carries ₦50 of overhead.

Before you change any price, set up three habits that make every later lesson easier: keep business money apart from household money, write things down, and protect yourself from payment fraud. None of these needs a computer. A notebook, a pen and your phone are enough.

Habit 1: separate business money

If sales money goes into the same purse or account as school fees and food money, you can never tell whether the business is making a profit. A simple fix is to open a separate account or wallet just for the business. Many sellers use a second account with their bank, or a business account with a provider such as Moniepoint, Opay or Paystack, so that every customer transfer lands in one place.

Then pay yourself on purpose. For example, decide that every Friday you move a fixed amount from the business account to your personal account as your wage. Whatever stays in the business account is for restocking and profit. This one habit makes your labour cost real.
Habit 2: write things down

You will need three short records: your **cost sheet** (from Lesson 2), a **price list** (what you charge for each item), and a **daily sales book** (what you sold each day). A notebook works well. If you prefer your phone, a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets lets you add up columns automatically. Module 3 shows the sales book in detail.

Keep your receipts too. Put market receipts, wholesaler invoices and transport notes in one envelope or snap a photo of each with your phone. When you sit down to recalculate your cost, the real numbers are right there, and you are not relying on memory. If a supplier does not give receipts, write the amount and date in your notebook as soon as you pay.

Also check what each payment method costs you. Some POS operators and payment providers charge a small fee on each transaction, and some customers ask you to pay for delivery or packaging separately. Find out the actual charges on the method you use and include them in your overhead, so that a sale paid by card or transfer does not quietly earn you less than a cash sale.
Habit 3: protect every payment

Transfers have made selling easier, but they have also brought scams. One of the most common in Nigeria is the **fake alert**: a buyer shows you a screenshot, or a fake SMS arrives, saying money has been sent, but no money has entered your account. Others pretend to overpay and ask for a refund of the difference. Some send a message that looks like it is from your bank and ask for your PIN or a code.

Rules that keep you safe

Only trust money you can see in your account balance inside your banking or wallet app. Never give anyone your PIN, password or one-time code (OTP), including people claiming to be from your bank. Do not refund an 'overpayment' until the full amount has truly arrived, and refund to the same account it came from. If a deal feels rushed, slow down.
Worked example: the Saturday rush

For example, Halima sells fabric at a busy market in Kano. On a Saturday a buyer picks ₦45,000 of fabric and says he has transferred the money. He shows a screenshot and is in a hurry. Figures are approximate.
Halima politely says, 'Thank you, let me just confirm it on my phone.'
She opens her bank app. Her balance has not changed.
She waits two minutes and refreshes. Still nothing.
She says, 'Sometimes transfers delay. You can wait, or pay by POS or cash.' She keeps the fabric folded beside her.
The buyer leaves without paying.
Halima loses nothing. A screenshot is easy to fake; her real balance is not. Saying 'let me confirm' calmly is normal business, not rudeness.

The simplest way to turn a cost into a price is **cost-plus pricing**: start from your true cost per item and add a chosen percentage on top. It is easy, it guarantees you never price below cost, and it is the right first step for almost every small seller. Its weakness is that it ignores what customers will pay, which is why Lesson 2 adds the market view. Here we master the arithmetic, because one small confusion costs sellers a lot of money.
Markup and margin: same profit, two percentages
Suppose a pack costs you ₦550 and you sell it for ₦800. Your profit is ₦250. You can describe that ₦250 in two ways:
**Markup** compares profit with **cost**: ₦250 ÷ ₦550 = 0.455, so a markup of about 45%.
**Margin** compares profit with **price**: ₦250 ÷ ₦800 = 0.3125, so a margin of about 31%.

Both are correct. They are just measured against different bases. Markup is always the bigger number because cost is smaller than price. Accountants and business advisers usually talk about margin; many traders in the market think in markup. Trouble starts when you mix them up.
Markup versus margin
Markup: profit over cost
Margin: profit over price
The same ₦250 profit is a 45% markup but only a 31% margin, because the bases are different.
Base is your cost
Price = cost × (1 + markup)
Always the larger percentage
Base is the selling price
Price = cost ÷ (1 − margin)
Shows share of each sale kept
The two formulas you need
To price with a **markup**: price = cost × (1 + markup). For a 50% markup on ₦550: ₦550 × 1.5 = ₦825.
To price with a **target margin**: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin). For a 40% margin on ₦550: ₦550 ÷ 0.6 = ₦916.67.
To check what you have: markup = profit ÷ cost, and margin = profit ÷ price.
Round your final price to a figure that is easy to pay and give change for, such as ₦800, ₦900 or ₦1,000, and recheck the margin after rounding.

How much markup is normal?

There is no single correct percentage. It depends on how fast items sell, how much risk you carry and how much skill is involved. Fast-moving goods that you simply buy and resell often carry a lower markup and make money through volume. Handmade items, services and goods that spoil or go out of fashion usually need a higher markup to cover time, waste and unsold stock. Rather than copying a 'standard' percentage, start with your true cost, test a margin you can live with, and compare it with the market in the next lesson.

Cost-plus pricing tells you the lowest price you can accept. It does not tell you what buyers will pay. Two more methods fill that gap. **Competitor-based pricing** looks at what similar sellers charge. **Value-based pricing** looks at what your product is worth to the customer. Good sellers use all three together: cost sets the floor, competitors show the range, value tells you where in the range, or above it, you belong.
Step 1: survey the market
List five to eight sellers your customers could buy from instead of you: in your market, on WhatsApp status, on Instagram, or in nearby shops.
Record each seller's price, size or quantity, and anything special (branding, delivery, freshness, location).
Compare like with like. Divide the price by the size to get the price per 100 g, per litre, or per piece.
Note the lowest, the middle and the highest price per unit. That is your market range.
Mark where your own price sits in that range.

Step 2: find your value

Value is what the customer gains, not what you put in. Ask yourself: what problem does my product solve, and what would the buyer lose if they did not buy from me? Common sources of value include **convenience** (delivery to the office, ready on time), **quality** (fresher, neater stitching, longer lasting), **reliability** (you always deliver what you promise), **personal service** (fitting, advice, follow-up) and **trust** (clean preparation, clear labels, NAFDAC registration where it is required for your product).
Ask three regular customers why they buy from you. Their words are your value.
Notice what customers praise or complain about in other sellers' reviews and comments.
List the extras you give that others do not, such as free delivery within an area or a quick adjustment after fitting.

For example, Amaka sews Ankara gowns. Her true cost is ₦11,000 per gown (Module 1). Local tailors charge roughly ₦12,000 to ₦25,000. Figures are approximate.
Cost floor: ₦11,000. A 30% margin would give ₦11,000 ÷ 0.7 = about ₦15,700.
Her value: a proper fitting, delivery in 3 days when many tailors take 2 weeks, and one free adjustment.
Customers who need an outfit for a wedding on Saturday value speed highly.
She sets her standard price at ₦18,000 and a rush price (48 hours) at ₦22,000.
Check: at ₦18,000 profit is ₦7,000 and margin is ₦7,000 ÷ ₦18,000 = 39%.
Amaka's price is above cost, inside the market range, and justified by real value she can explain to every customer.
Prices must still be honest

Value-based pricing means charging for real benefits you deliver. It never means exaggerating quality, inventing claims, or charging one customer far more for the same thing just because she looks rich. That damages trust quickly.

Be careful about racing to the bottom. If a competitor is much cheaper, find out why before you react: smaller size, lower quality inputs, no labour counted, or a different customer group. Matching a price you cannot afford only moves you from making a profit to making a loss. Often the better answer is to stay at your price and explain your difference clearly, or to offer a smaller, cheaper size for price-sensitive buyers.

If your cost-plus price is far above the whole market range, either your costs are too high (look for cheaper inputs, bulk buying or less waste), or you must clearly offer extra value. If your price is far below the range, you may be leaving profit on the table.

Decide when to say no to a discount request

A discount feels small to the customer, but it comes straight out of your profit, not out of your cost. That is why a 10% price cut can wipe out a third or more of what you earn on each item. Before you give any discount, you should know exactly what it costs you.
Why a small discount bites hard

Take Ngozi's pack again: price ₦800, true cost ₦550, profit ₦250. If she gives 10% off, the price falls by ₦80 to ₦720. Her cost does not change, so her profit falls from ₦250 to ₦170. The customer saved 10%, but Ngozi lost 32% of her profit on that pack.

The extra-sales rule

To earn the same total profit after a discount, divide the old profit per item by the new profit per item. That tells you how many times more items you must sell. At 10% off: ₦250 ÷ ₦170 = 1.47. So if Ngozi normally sells 100 packs a week, she must sell about 147 packs at the discounted price just to stand still. At 20% off she would need about 278 packs. Ask yourself honestly: will the discount really bring that many more buyers?

Calculate new profit

A quick calculation before every discount stops you trading hard for less money.
Worked example: a bulk order from an office
For example, an office manager asks Ngozi for 30 packs every Friday and wants a discount. Figures are approximate.
Normally each pack carries about ₦50 of delivery and data overhead because she delivers small orders separately.
With one delivery for 30 packs, her overhead per pack drops to about ₦20, so her true cost falls from ₦550 to about ₦520.
She offers ₦750 per pack for orders of 30 or more.
Profit per pack: ₦750 − ₦520 = ₦230. On 30 packs that is ₦6,900 every Friday.
Margin check: ₦230 ÷ ₦750 = 31%, almost the same as her normal margin.
This is a good discount: it is paid for by a real cost saving and guaranteed volume, not by her own profit.
Better ways to say 'special offer'

**Add value instead of cutting price.** 'Buy 10, get 1 free' sounds generous. On 10 packs at ₦800 she receives ₦8,000; the 11 packs cost her 11 × ₦550 = ₦6,050; profit ₦1,950. A 10% discount on 10 packs gives ₦7,200 minus ₦5,500 = only ₦1,700. The free item costs her its cost, not its price.
**Discount for a reason you control:** bulk quantity, early payment, collection instead of delivery, or a slow day of the week.
**Set a time limit** such as 'this weekend only', so the lower price does not become the new normal.
**Bundle** a slow item with a popular one rather than cutting the popular item's price.
A price tag label
Every discount on the label comes straight out of your profit, so plan it on paper first.
Never discount below your floor
If a discount takes your price under your true cost, every extra sale makes you poorer. It is better to lose that one sale politely than to train customers to expect a loss-making price.
Decide your limits before the customer asks

Write your normal price, your best bulk price and your walk-away price for each item. In a busy moment, you will not have time to calculate, and a written limit stops you agreeing to something you regret.
The opposite also works: small price rises

The extra-sales rule works in reverse. If Ngozi raises her price by 10%, from ₦800 to ₦880, her profit per pack rises from ₦250 to ₦330. Divide the old profit by the new: ₦250 ÷ ₦330 = 0.76. She could sell about 24% fewer packs and still earn the same total profit, with less work and fewer ingredients. That does not mean every price rise is wise, but it shows why a careful increase is often less risky than sellers fear, and why a discount is often more costly than it looks.

In open markets where bargaining is expected, think in naira, not percentages. Know how many naira of profit each item carries, decide how many of those naira you are willing to give up, and stop there. A customer who bargains you down from ₦800 to ₦700 has taken ₦100 of your ₦250 profit, which is 40% of it.

Finally, watch what discounts teach your customers. If you cut prices every time someone hesitates, buyers learn to hesitate. If you discount only for clear reasons, they learn that your price is fair and that the way to pay less is to buy more or commit regularly.

The selling conversation: from greeting to 'yes'
Lead a selling conversation in five clear stages
Turn product features into customer benefits
State your price clearly without apologising
Ask for the sale and arrange payment and delivery

A good price only becomes money when someone buys. Selling is not about pressure or clever tricks. It is a short, friendly conversation in which you find out what the customer needs, show how your product meets that need, state your price clearly and make it easy to say yes. The same stages work face to face in the market, on the phone and on WhatsApp.
Five stages of a sale
Greet and connect
Ask about needs
Show benefits
State the price
Ask for the sale
Most lost sales skip stage 2 or stage 5: sellers talk before listening, or never actually ask the customer to buy.
Stage 1: greet and connect

Greet warmly and use the customer's name if you know it. In person, smile and give your full attention; put the phone down. On WhatsApp, reply as quickly as you can, because a buyer who waits a long time often buys elsewhere. A short, polite opening is enough: 'Good afternoon, Mrs Bello. Thank you for your message. How can I help you today?'
Stage 2: ask before you tell

Ask two or three simple questions to understand what she wants. **Who is it for? When does she need it? What matters most to her: size, taste, style, speed or price?** Her answers tell you which product to suggest and which benefits to talk about. A customer buying chin chin for a child's birthday party cares about quantity and delivery time; one buying a gift cares about packaging.
Stage 3: show benefits, not just features
A **feature** is a fact about the product. A **benefit** is what that fact does for the customer. Customers buy benefits. Always link the two with the words 'which means'.
Feature
Benefit (which means...)
Fried fresh on the morning of delivery
It is crunchy and tastes homemade when your guests eat it
Sealed pack with a label
It stays fresh for days and looks neat as a gift
Gown finished in 3 days with one free adjustment
You will be ready for Saturday's wedding and it will fit perfectly
Delivery to your office
You do not need to leave work or pay for transport
Two people talking about a product
Listening first lets you talk about the benefits that matter to this customer.
Stage 4: state the price clearly

Say the price plainly, with the benefit next to it, then stop talking. 'The 200 gram pack is ₦800, fried fresh and delivered to your office.' Do not add 'I know it is a bit much' or 'but I can reduce'. Apologising tells the buyer you do not believe in your own price, and invites bargaining. A short silence after the price is normal; let the customer think.
Practise your price out loud
Say your price and one benefit ten times in front of a mirror or to a friend, until it sounds calm and normal. Many sellers find their voice shakes the first few times. Practice is the cure.
Stage 5: ask for the sale

When the customer seems interested, ask a simple closing question that moves things forward: 'How many packs would you like?', 'Shall I deliver on Thursday or Friday?' or 'Would you like to pay by transfer or cash on delivery?' These questions assume the sale politely and make the next step easy. Then confirm the details: item, quantity, price, total, payment method, delivery day and address.
Worked example: a WhatsApp enquiry
For example, Funmi asks Ngozi on WhatsApp: 'How much is your chin chin?' Figures are approximate.
Greet: 'Good morning Funmi, thank you for asking!'
Ask: 'Is it for yourself, an office, or an event? When do you need it?' Funmi says it is for a birthday party of about 25 children on Saturday.
Benefit: 'For a party, the 200 g packs work well. Each child gets their own sealed pack, fried fresh on Friday.'
Price: '₦800 per pack. For 25 packs that is ₦20,000, delivered to you on Saturday morning.'
Close: 'Would you like me to book 25 packs for you? I take a 50% deposit (₦10,000) to confirm, and the balance on delivery.'
Funmi pays the deposit. Ngozi checks her bank app, sees the ₦10,000, and sends a written confirmation of the order.
After the sale
Thank the customer and confirm the order in writing (a WhatsApp message is fine).
Deliver exactly what you promised, on time. If there is a delay, tell her early.
Follow up a day later: 'Did the children enjoy it?' This builds trust and often brings the next order.
Ask happy customers if you can share their kind words, and save their number for future offers.

If you use the free WhatsApp Business app, you can set up a short catalogue with photos and prices, quick replies for common questions and labels to track new orders and paid orders. These features save time, but the five stages above still do the selling.

Handling price objections and bargaining honestly

An **objection** is a reason a customer gives for not buying yet. Objections are normal and often a good sign: a customer who objects is still interested enough to talk. Most objections are about price, trust or timing. The goal is not to win an argument but to understand the real concern and answer it honestly.
A four-step method for any objection
Respond to an objection
Listen fully
Acknowledge the concern
Ask a clarifying question
Respond with value or options
After responding, check if the concern is settled; if not, go round again calmly.
**Listen** to the whole objection without interrupting or defending yourself.
**Acknowledge** it respectfully: 'I understand, you want to be sure it is worth the money.'
**Ask** a question to find the real concern: 'Is it the total amount, or are you comparing with another seller?'
**Respond** with value, a different option, or honest facts. Then check: 'Does that help?'

Notice that none of the good responses starts with a price cut. When you reduce the price at the first sign of hesitation, you lose profit and you also suggest that your first price was not honest. Offering a smaller size, a different style or a payment plan keeps your price per item intact while still helping the customer who truly has a smaller budget.
Bargaining in the market

In many Nigerian markets, buyers expect to bargain, and refusing completely can seem unfriendly. The answer is to plan. For each item, decide three numbers in advance: your **asking price**, your **target price** and your **walk-away price**. The walk-away price must be above your true cost. Start at the asking price, move slowly and in small steps, and give something only when you get something, such as a bigger quantity or immediate payment.
Worked example: bargaining over a gown
For example, a customer asks Amaka to sew a gown. Amaka's true cost is ₦11,000. Her plan: asking ₦18,000, target ₦17,000, walk-away ₦15,000. Figures are approximate.
Amaka listens and acknowledges: 'I understand you want a good price.' She asks: 'When do you need it?' The customer needs it for a wedding in 4 days.
Amaka responds with value: 'I will fit you on Wednesday and deliver on Friday, with one free adjustment. Many tailors will not finish in time.'
Customer: 'Make it ₦15,000.' Amaka offers ₦17,000 if paid in full today.
They agree at ₦17,000 with full payment, which Amaka confirms in her bank app.
Profit is ₦17,000 − ₦11,000 = ₦6,000, a 35% margin. Amaka stayed above her walk-away price and gave a reason for every move.
Do not split the difference by reflex

If the customer offers half your price and you meet in the middle each time, you will end up far below your plan. Move in small steps, and only in exchange for something, such as full payment, a bigger order or collection instead of delivery.
Selling honestly
Describe your product truthfully. Do not claim it 'cures', 'whitens' or 'lasts forever' if you cannot prove it.
Give the full weight, quantity or size you advertise, and use accurate scales.
Treat customers fairly: the same item should carry the same price for similar customers on the same terms.
Be honest about delivery time. Promise what you can do, then do it.
If something goes wrong, admit it and fix it quickly: replace, refund or repair.

Honesty is also good business. Word of mouth and WhatsApp status travel fast; one unhappy customer who feels cheated can cost you many sales. Nigeria also has a federal consumer protection agency, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), which handles consumer complaints, another reason to deal fairly.
It is fine to lose some sales
Not every buyer is your customer. If someone only wants a price below your cost, wish her well. Losing a sale that would have lost you money is a win.

**Sales amount** = quantity × price. **Profit** here means gross profit: sales amount minus quantity × true cost. Because your true cost already includes your wage and an overhead share, this profit is what the business truly earned. In the example, Monday's margin is ₦11,100 ÷ ₦35,700 = 31%.

Writing every sale down each day shows your real profit, not just money in hand.
A weekly summary
Every week, add up your daily pages and write a short summary. Five numbers tell you most of what you need to know:
**Total sales (revenue):** all money from sales this week.
**Total gross profit:** sales minus the true cost of the items sold.
**Margin:** gross profit ÷ sales. Compare it with the margin you planned. If it is falling, find out why.
**Discounts given:** total naira given away in discounts and bargaining.
**Best and slowest items:** which products sold most and which barely moved.

Each month: compare and review

Break-even: how much must you sell?

Some costs are fixed: they stay the same no matter how much you sell, such as monthly shop rent, a market levy or a staff salary. Your **break-even point** is the number of items you must sell to cover those fixed costs. The formula is: fixed costs ÷ profit per item (price minus the cost of making one item).
Worked example: should Ngozi rent a kiosk?
For example, Ngozi is offered a small kiosk near an office complex for about ₦30,000 a month. She currently sells from home. Figures are approximate.
Her profit per pack (price ₦800 minus true cost ₦550) is ₦250.
Break-even: ₦30,000 ÷ ₦250 = 120 packs a month just to pay the kiosk rent.
That is about 5 extra packs a day over 24 trading days.
Her records show walk-in buyers at a similar spot bought about 10 packs a day when she tested a table there for a week.
Expected extra profit: (10 − 5) × ₦250 × 24 days = ₦30,000 a month after rent.
Because her records gave her a real number for daily sales, Ngozi can decide using facts, not hope. She takes the kiosk and checks after one month whether sales match the test.
Two more numbers worth tracking

**Enquiries versus sales.** Keep a simple tally of how many people ask about your product (in person, by phone or on WhatsApp) and how many actually buy. If 20 people ask in a week and 4 buy, 1 in 5 enquiries becomes a sale. If many people ask but few buy, look at your selling conversation, your photos or how you state the price. If few people ask at all, the problem is more likely visibility than price.

**Repeat customers.** Put a small mark next to the name of anyone who buys again. Repeat buyers are the cheapest sales you will ever make, because you do not have to find them again. If your repeat customers keep coming back after a price rise, that is strong evidence your price is fair.

At the end of each day, also count the cash in your bag and compare it with the cash sales you wrote down, and check that transfers in your app match the transfer sales in your book. If the numbers do not agree, find the gap that same day while you still remember the sales.
Watch your margin, not just your sales

Sales can rise while profit falls, for example when input prices go up but your price stays the same, or when you give more discounts. A falling margin in your weekly summary is your early warning to recalculate costs.
Use what you already have

If customers pay by transfer, your bank or wallet app keeps a history you can check against your sales book. Many POS and payment providers also show daily totals. Cash sales still need writing down, because they leave no trail.

Common errors to check

Did you divide by good items, not total items? Did you include your labour and overhead? Did you use margin and markup correctly? Is your walk-away price above your true cost? Are your input prices from the last month, not last year?

If you sell more than one product

Make one sheet for your main product first. Then repeat the cost calculation for each other item, because different items carry different costs and margins. You may find that one item you thought was popular earns very little, while a quieter item is your best earner. That knowledge helps you decide what to promote and what to reprice or drop.

If you sell a service, do the same with one standard job. You can also set an hourly or daily rate: true cost per hour (your hourly labour rate plus overhead per hour), divided by one minus your target margin. For example, ₦1,000 labour plus ₦250 overhead is ₦1,250 per hour; for a 35% margin, ₦1,250 ÷ 0.65 = about ₦1,920, so roughly ₦2,000 an hour.

A price is not set once and forgotten. Costs change, your skill and reputation grow, and customers' needs shift. This final lesson helps you build a 90-day plan so that reviewing your price becomes a routine, not a crisis. It also walks you through checking your capstone evidence before you take the final quiz.
When to review your price
**On a fixed schedule:** for example, at the end of every month, using your weekly summaries.
**When a major input price moves:** if the price of a main ingredient, material or transport changes noticeably, recalculate that week.
**When your margin falls:** if your weekly margin drops a few points below your plan for two or three weeks.
**When demand changes:** if you are always sold out (you may be underpriced) or sales slow sharply (check price, quality and visibility).
The pricing review loop
Record sales and costs
Review margin monthly
Recalculate true cost
Adjust price or offer
Communicate the change
Each 30-day loop keeps your price matched to your real costs and market.
Reading your records

At each review, look at four things side by side: your current true cost, your margin for the month, the number of items sold, and the discounts you gave. A healthy picture is a steady or rising margin with steady sales. If margin is falling while sales are steady, costs have probably risen. If sales fall after a price rise, check whether the fall is larger than the extra-sales rule says you can afford (Module 2, Lesson 3) before deciding to reverse it.

For example, this is how Ngozi uses the review loop over three months. Figures are approximate.
Month 1: sells 220 packs at ₦800. True cost ₦550. Margin 31%, as planned. She notes that office bulk orders are her steadiest sales.
Month 2: flour and oil rise; true cost becomes ₦600. Margin falls to 25%. She gives two weeks' notice and moves to ₦850.
Month 3: sells 205 packs at ₦850. Profit per pack ₦250, total ₦51,250, compared with ₦55,000 in Month 1 and only ₦44,000 if she had stayed at ₦800 on 220 packs.
She also notices the 100 g pack has a lower margin and sells slowly, so she plans to review its price next month.
Without the review, Month 3 profit at the old price would have been lower even with more sales. With it, her margin is back to 29% and she has a clear next step.

Do not change your price every week. Frequent small changes confuse customers and make it hard to tell what is working. Unless a cost rises sharply, keep a price for at least a month, collect the records, and then decide. One clear change backed by numbers is better than many nervous adjustments.

Why this matters
Cost, price and profit
Cost: what it takes you to make or buy it
Price: what the customer pays you
Profit: price minus cost
Revenue is not profit
Every sale has three numbers behind it.
Cost is the money, and time, it takes you to make or buy the thing you sell.
Price is what the customer pays you.
Profit is what is left when you take cost away from price.
If a pack of chin chin costs you 550 naira to make and you sell it for 800 naira, your profit is 250 naira.
But if you sell it for 500 naira, you are losing 50 naira on every pack, even if your purse feels full.
Money coming in is called revenue. Revenue is not profit.
Common mistakes
Counting only materials
Copying the next seller's price
Never reviewing the price
The first mistake is counting only materials.
Many sellers add up flour, sugar and oil, then stop. They forget packaging, transport, gas, phone data, and most of all, their own hours of work.
The second mistake is copying the next seller's price.
She may buy in bulk, pay no rent, or be losing money without knowing it. Her price tells you about the market, not about your cost.
The third mistake is never reviewing your price.
Flour, cooking gas and transport can change quickly. A price that gave a good profit six months ago can quietly turn into a loss.
Step by step
Direct costs: materials and packaging
Labour: your hours at a fair hourly rate
Overhead share: rent, data, transport
Allow for waste and samples
Divide by the number of good items
Here is the method. First, add your direct costs for one batch. These are the things that go into or onto the product, like ingredients, gas and packaging.
Use what you actually paid, from your receipts, not what you hope to pay.
Second, add your labour. Ask what you could earn doing similar work for someone else.
If a day's work of 8 hours pays about 8,000 naira, your hour is worth about 1,000 naira.
Third, add a share of overhead. That is stall rent, market levy, fuel, data, transport and POS charges. Add them for a month and share them across everything you make.
Fourth, allow for waste. If 2 of every 40 packs are spoiled or tasted, divide by 38, not 40.
Finally, divide the batch total by the number of good items.
The answer is your price floor. Below it, you lose money on every sale.

Three views of price
Cost, competitors and value
Cost-plus: the lowest safe price
Competitors: the market range

In Module 1 you found your true cost. Now you turn it into a price.
Cost-plus pricing starts from your cost and adds a chosen percentage. It tells you the lowest price you can accept.
Competitor pricing looks at what similar sellers charge.
Value pricing looks at what your product is worth to the customer. Good sellers use all three together.
And before you give any discount, you will know exactly what it costs you.
Markup
Profit over cost
250 on 550 is about 45%
Always the bigger number
Margin
Profit over price
250 on 800 is about 31%
Share of each sale you keep
Say a pack costs you 550 naira and you sell it for 800 naira. Your profit is 250 naira.
Markup compares that profit with your cost. 250 divided by 550 is a markup of about 45%.
Margin compares the same profit with your price. 250 divided by 800 is a margin of about 31%.
Both are correct. Trouble starts when you mix them up.
Step by step
Pricing for a target margin
Adding 30% to cost does not give you a 30% margin.
Start with your true cost per item
Price = cost divided by (1 minus margin)
Round to an easy price to pay
Recheck profit and margin after rounding
Here is the method. Start with your true cost per item from Module 1.
To keep a target margin, divide your cost by 1 minus that margin. For a 30% margin on 550 naira, divide 550 by 0.70. That gives about 785 naira.
Round to a figure that is easy to pay and give change for, such as 800 naira.
Then recheck. Rounding up is usually safe, but rounding down can eat your margin.
Now the trap. If you simply add 30% to 550 naira, you get 715 naira. Your real margin is only 23%, not 30%.

Where value comes from
Convenience: delivered, ready on time
Quality: fresher, neater, longer lasting

Personal service and trust
Value is what the customer gains, not what you put in. Convenience is one source, like delivery to the office.

In many markets buyers expect to bargain, so plan before you start.
Amaka decides an asking price of 18,000 naira, a target of 17,000 naira, and a walk-away price of 15,000 naira, which is above her cost.

Sell honestly
Honest selling builds repeat sales
Do
Describe the product truthfully
Give the full weight you advertise
Promise only what you can do
Do not
Claim it cures or lasts forever
Meet in the middle every time
Go below your walk-away price
Sell honestly. Describe your product truthfully, give the full quantity you advertise, and be honest about delivery time.
Do not make claims you cannot prove. Do not meet in the middle each time, or you will end far below your plan. Move in small steps, and only for something in return, like full payment.
If a buyer only wants a price below your cost, wish her well.

Records turn guesses into facts. Write each sale: date, item, quantity, price, sales amount, cost, profit and how she paid.
On Monday, Ngozi sold 12 packs at 800 naira, 30 bulk packs at 750 naira, and 8 small packs at 450 naira.
Her sales were 35,700 naira and her profit was 11,100 naira. That is a margin of 31%, just as she planned.
Check your cash and your app against the book the same day.
Every week
Your five-number weekly summary
Total sales
Total gross profit
Margin: profit divided by sales
Discounts given
Best and slowest items
Each week, write five numbers: total sales, gross profit, margin, discounts given, and your best and slowest items.
Sales can rise while profit falls. A falling margin is your early warning to recalculate costs.
Key points
Remember
Greet, ask, show benefits, state price, ask for the sale
Listen, acknowledge, ask, then respond

Write every sale and check your margin weekly
Break-even = fixed costs divided by profit per item
To remember. Follow the five stages and ask for the sale. Answer objections calmly before you ever cut a price. Plan your three prices. Write every sale.
And to see if a fixed cost like rent is worth it, divide it by your profit per item.

This module brings everything together. First, a one-page pricing sheet that shows exactly how your price was set and why.
Second, a record of a real or practised selling conversation using that price.
Third, a 90-day plan for reviewing your price. Your certificate should reflect a price you actually calculated, not one you guessed.
Step by step
Every offer and walk-away price must stay above cost.
Two or three value points
Chosen price, profit, markup, margin
Bulk, promotion and walk-away prices
Date made and next review date
Here is what goes on the sheet. First, your true cost from Module 1: direct costs, labour, overhead and waste.
Second, the market range from your survey: lowest, middle and highest price per unit.
Third, the two or three benefits customers told you they value most.
Fourth, your chosen price, with its profit, markup and margin.
Fifth, your bulk price, any promotion, and your walk-away price, each with its profit.
Sixth, the date you made the sheet and the date of your next review. If any part is missing, your price is partly a guess.

Labour and overhead included

Check your sheet. Did you divide by good items? Did you include labour and overhead? Did you use markup and margin correctly? Is your walk-away price above cost? Are your input prices from the last month, not last year?
Then ask a trusted person to check it too.
Show your price
Presenting your price
Builds trust
One price list for everyone
Size, price and one benefit
Same price on every channel
Loses trust
DM for price
Price changes person to person
Shrinking a pack quietly
Customers judge your price partly by how you present it. Share one clear price list with everyone, with the size, price and one short benefit for each item.
Keep the same price on your stall and your WhatsApp catalogue.
Answering DM for price makes some buyers move on. Prices that change from person to person feel suspicious. And reducing the quantity quietly without telling customers damages trust.
Raising a price
A respectful price increase
For example, Ngozi's flour and oil costs rise, and her margin at 800 naira falls to 25%.
New true cost per pack
New price from 1 November
Orders placed before then
Sometimes your price must go up. Handled well, most regular customers accept it.
Ngozi's true cost rises to 600 naira. For a 30% margin she divides 600 by 0.70, gets 857, and chooses 850 naira.
Two weeks ahead she sends her regulars a short, honest message, and she honours every order placed before the date at the old price.
Her new margin is 29%, and most regulars stay.
Every 30 days
On a fixed schedule, every month
When a main input price moves
When your margin falls for weeks
When demand changes sharply
A price is not set once and forgotten. Review it at the end of every month, using your weekly summaries.
Recalculate that week if a main ingredient, material or transport price changes noticeably.
Review if your margin drops below your plan for two or three weeks.
And review if you always sell out, or if sales slow sharply.
But do not change your price every week. Keep a price for at least a month, then decide with your records.
Key points
Remember
One page: cost, market, value, price, offers, dates
Write one sentence explaining your price
One price list, the same on every channel
Give notice of increases; honour existing orders
Review monthly and when key costs move

To remember. Put cost, market, value, price, offers and dates on one page, and explain your price in one sentence. Share one clear price list. Give notice before a price rise. And review your price every month.
